body: At twenty past five in the morning a minicab driver is third in the queue on an airport rank, which means about forty minutes of nothing. There is a link in his messages from a fare last week, from one of those conversations that went on longer than either of them expected, and he has not opened it because he assumed it wanted something from him. This morning he does. Something starts playing, and while it plays he taps about to find out what he has landed on — who is behind it, what else is on there, what the numbers down the side mean. He is halfway through reading when he notices that the music has not stopped. He goes back to the queue two cars later with it still going.
That is the whole trick, and it is a small one. He was not made to choose before he was allowed to hear anything, and he was not punished with silence for being curious about what he was hearing.

The plainest way in is to press play on anything at all and then carry on browsing. The player sits at the bottom of every page and does not stop when you navigate — read an article, open another station, go through the entire catalogue, and the sound continues underneath it.

It is worth being literal about what a radio actually was, because that is what is being rebuilt here without the hardware. A radio was four things: a dial you could move without reading anything, bands that grouped stations by kind, a speaker that stayed on while you did something else, and a set that lived in one place so the household knew where it was. Not one of those four is about content. All four are about the object holding still while a life goes on around it. A band you cannot buy a radio for has to supply the same four things out of a browser, and the hardest of them, by a distance, is the third.
The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. Every station holds one frequency, no two share a number, and each one has its own page and its own address.

Keeping the sound alive across a whole site is more work than it appears from the outside, and it is the piece most things of this kind get wrong. One player, one stream, one piece of state carried from page to page, so that moving through the site is moving around a house with the radio on rather than opening and closing separate rooms. Press play once and it keeps playing wherever you go on the site. That is the whole design, and everything else here is arranged to protect it.

This is rarer than it should be. The ordinary experience now is that a page wants something before it gives you anything — accept this, install the app, make an account, allow notifications — and then, when you finally do get some audio, it dies the moment you tap through to find out what you are listening to. The medium punishes curiosity. Nobody decided that; it is what happens when every surface is designed to capture a decision rather than to be lived alongside. A radio never asked you a single question in its life.

The categories along the top are the bands. There are the music stations, which are most of the dial. There are the teaching and prayer frequencies. There are the family-safe formats. And there is the international stretch, hosted in its own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every station has a page of its own saying what it is for, who hosts it, and what is playing on it at this moment, which is the equivalent of the printed schedule that used to sit beside the set.
Which leaves the one thing a broadcast band does that no library has ever managed, and it is not a technical matter. It is a social one.

Be fair to the playlist first, because it is superb at the job it has. If you know what you want, a search box will find it in seconds and nothing else comes close. But look at what happens when you try to give a playlist to somebody. What you send them is a link into your own library, which opens an app they may not have, behind an account they may not want, and which arrives as a small statement about your taste that they are now expected to have an opinion about. It is a recommendation, and recommendations create a debt. Half of them are never opened for exactly that reason.
A link to a station is not a recommendation. It is a frequency, and you can simply hand it over.

Just before eleven at night a woman in her thirties, sitting on the edge of the bath because it is the only room with a lock on it, sends her brother a text with nothing in it but a number and a station name. He is four time zones away and two hours into a twelve-hour shift on a loading bay, and he reads it on his break and does not reply, because they are not the sort of family that replies. He puts it on. She has it on too, at low volume, in a house where everybody else is asleep. Neither of them mentions it the next week, or the week after, and both of them keep it on.
Nothing was asked for there and nothing had to be answered. A frequency is handed over the way you tell somebody where a good bench is — here is a place, it will be there, do as you like.

It has to be said that a browser is not a wireless set, and pretending otherwise would be silly. Close the tab and it stops. A phone locks itself, a data connection drops in a lift, and there is no dial to turn with your thumb while your other hand is in the washing-up. Nothing here is going to sit on a windowsill for thirty years and outlive you, which is a genuine thing that radios did and this cannot do.

But the trade is very much better than it looks. The set is already in everybody’s pocket, and it was not bought for this. There is no hardware to obtain, no shipping, no aerial and no waiting — which means the band is available tonight to somebody on an inexpensive phone in a place where nobody is going to be posting radios. What has been lost is the object. What has been gained is that a frequency arrives in a text message and starts playing eight seconds later, anywhere. That is the swap, and it was taken deliberately.

So the practical summary is unglamorous. Press play on anything. Wander about while it keeps playing. Use the categories as bands rather than as a menu, learn roughly where things sit, and let a station page tell you what you have found. When something is worth passing on, copy the link and send the number to one person. That is the entire manual, and there is no hidden second half.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. No queue to build and no decision to make before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 376.20 — Melody’s Sparkle. It is the easiest station on the band to leave running while you learn your way round the rest of it: gratitude, family and everyday wonder, clean and warm and never preachy, written to be playable to somebody who is not in church and is not being worked on. That makes it the natural first frequency for the thing this article has been describing, because it is the one you can hand to anybody — a colleague, a neighbour, a brother on a loading bay — without it landing as an argument. Press play on it, then go and turn the dial with it still going, and you will have understood the design inside a minute.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. What it does is keep your favourites and follows with you across every Jubilee site, and tell this band which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for — which is how the next station gets chosen and how this one gets better.

So take this as an invitation rather than a set of instructions, because there is almost nothing to instruct. Put HM 376.20 on this afternoon and then go wandering through the dial with it playing underneath you, the way you would wander round a house. Add the page to your home screen so it is where the radio used to be. And when you find the frequency that belongs in your kitchen, send the number to one person who would never have gone looking for it. That is how a band spreads, and it always was.
